old:
Compose's smart recomposition decision rule:

> When a parent recomposes, for each child `@Composable` call:
> 1. Are all parameters **stable** types?
> 2. If yes — compare each with `equals()` to its previous value.
> 3. If none changed — **skip** the child's body entirely.
> 4. If any parameter is unstable — **always re-run** the child, regardless.

That last point is the killer. **One unstable parameter forces every recomposition.** A `LazyColumn` with 1000 rows that pass an unstable `List` will recompose every row, every frame, every time anything changes.

Smart recomposition is what makes Compose performant. Stability is what unlocks it. Get this wrong and Compose performs worse than the View system you migrated from.
new:
With strong skipping enabled (the default since Kotlin 2.0.20), restartable composables can be skipped even with unstable parameters. Stable arguments compare with `equals()`; unstable arguments compare by reference identity (`===`). An invalidated scope still runs.

A list recreated on each parent recomposition is a different reference even when its contents are equal. Reusing an unchanged instance can permit skipping; it does not make mutation observable. Under the older non-strong-skipping model, unstable parameters made a composable unskippable.

Use compiler reports and runtime measurements to distinguish input changes, state invalidation and expensive work. Stability alone does not establish a frame-rate outcome.
reason: Replace legacy universal skipping rules with the current versioned comparison model.
approval: Owner requested verified official-source fixes and publication, 2026-10-27; source-repository PR additionally requested.

old: > Skippable recomposition is the difference between a buttery 60fps Compose UI and a stuttery one. The compiler decides what's skippable based on **stability**. Most perf bugs in production Compose apps trace to a single unstable parameter forcing an entire sub-tree to recompose every frame. Staff-level mastery is reading the Compose compiler metrics, knowing exactly which types are inferred stable, knowing when to annotate `@Immutable` vs `@Stable`, and using `ImmutableList` for collections — all without breaking the cache.
new: > Compose can skip eligible work when inputs compare unchanged. Stability, identity reuse, state observation and the compiler mode determine that decision. Learn to read compiler reports, choose honest `@Immutable`/`@Stable` contracts and measure the work that actually affects a frame.

old:
5. **Why is `@HiltViewModel` scoped to `ActivityRetainedComponent` rather than `ActivityComponent`?**
   ViewModels are designed by the Android framework to survive configuration changes (rotation). `ActivityComponent` is destroyed on rotation. Therefore, ViewModels must live in `ActivityRetainedComponent`, which maps to that exact rotation-surviving lifetime.
new:
5. **Which component supplies a Hilt ViewModel, and why can it not depend on an ActivityComponent-scoped object?**
   Hilt uses ViewModelComponent for each ViewModel. ViewModelComponent and ActivityComponent are siblings beneath ActivityRetainedComponent. A ViewModel can use bindings from its own component and ancestors, not the Activity sibling. ViewModelStore ownership lets it survive Activity recreation without retaining the old Activity.
reason: Correct the repeated Hilt ViewModel ownership explanation.
approval: Owner requested official-source fixes, publication and an original-repository PR, 2026-10-27.

old: Annotating everything `@Singleton` forces the app to keep every class in RAM indefinitely, leading to massive memory bloat and slower startup times. Instead, most classes should be unscoped (so they can be garbage collected when the referencing component dies) or scoped tightly to the ViewModel (`@ViewModelScoped`).
new: A scoped binding is created when requested and its component caches the result. Scope does not eagerly construct all classes, but an app-wide cached object can retain state longer than needed. Choose scope from actual sharing and ownership requirements; use startup traces to establish initialization cost.
reason: Fix the answer-key claim about eager creation of all singleton bindings.
approval: Owner requested official-source fixes, publication and an original-repository PR, 2026-10-27.

old:
5. **What are "Expedited Jobs" in WorkManager, and what specific Android 12+ restriction were they introduced to bypass?**
   They allow immediate, high-priority background execution. They were introduced to bypass Android 12's restriction that prevents apps running in the background from launching Foreground Services.
new:
5. **What does an expedited WorkRequest request, and what happens when its quota is unavailable?**
   It requests prompt execution for short, important work within system quota. Use setExpedited with an OutOfQuotaPolicy to choose ordinary-work fallback or dropping the request. It does not guarantee immediate execution or exempt arbitrary background work from platform restrictions.
reason: Correct the repeated immediate-execution guarantee.

old: Because Gradle's incremental build and caching are mathematically designed to be 100% reliable based on inputs/outputs. If `clean` is required to fix a build, it means a task is failing to declare its inputs/outputs correctly, polluting the cache. Fixing the broken task is the real solution.
new: Correct task inputs, outputs and dependencies support reliable incremental builds and cache reuse. Repeated clean-only recovery is a diagnostic signal, not proof of a mathematically corrupt graph: investigate stale outputs, task declarations, plugin defects and environmental differences. Clean removes project outputs, not the shared build cache.
reason: Align the answer key with the corrected output/cache distinction.
approval: Owner requested official-source fixes, publication and an original-repository PR, 2026-10-27.

old: ## Diagnosing Slow Startup
new:
## Diagnosing Slow Startup

For an app shipping native code, also check [16 KB page-size compatibility](../../release-engineering/16kb-page-sizes.md). Android 15 introduced support for devices configured with 16 KB pages. Audit your own and SDK-provided native libraries, ELF and APK alignment, and test in a 16 KB environment. This compatibility check complements startup traces; it is not a promise of a specific startup-speed improvement. See the [official page-size guide](https://developer.android.com/guide/practices/page-sizes).
reason: Add the requested native-library compatibility cross-reference without claiming all Android 15 devices use 16 KB pages.
